Should White choose to play e4 because our knight on f6 is still pinned...

We should immediately pose a question to the bishop in order to break the pin.

r2qk2r/pbpp2bp/np2pnp1/3P1p2/2P2B2/2N2NP.text:
Bf4 develops the bishop for White.

We can calmly castle.

r2qk2r/pbpp2bp/np2pnp1/3P1p2/2PN4/2N3P1/.text:
Nd4 converges on our pawn.

We will castle, sacrificing a pawn!

r2qk2r/pbpp2bp/np2pnp1/3P1pB1/2P5/2N2NP1.text:
Bg5 pins us. Don't move the knight!

We will castle.

r4rk1/p1pq2bp/1p3np1/2n2p2/2PN4/2N3P1/PP.text: We recapture with the queen, connecting rooks and completing our development. We have pressure on the knight and on the open e and d files, so getting some compensation for that pawn should be no problem at all.

r4rk1/pbpp1qb1/np2p1pp/3PPp2/2P5/2N2NP1/.text:
White adds a defender to e5.

We add a potential attacker by bringing a rook to e8, as after exd5 we would open up an attack on the e5-pawn.

r4rk1/pbpp2b1/np2pqpp/3PPp2/2P5/2N2NP1/P.text:
e5, closing down the diagonal and attacking the queen seems reasonable for White.

But we stay near the action of the kingside on f7.

rn1Qk2r/pbp3bp/1p2pnp1/5p2/2P5/5NP1/PP2P.text:
Remember that trades benefit the side with less space.

We recapture.

rn1k3r/pbp3bp/1p2pnp1/5p2/2P5/5NP1/PP2PP.text:
Not all checks are scary, you know.

Sidestepping is a valid continuation. Furthermore, we defend our bishop against any discoveries from the knight.

rn1q1rk1/pbp3bp/1p1ppnp1/5p2/2PP1B2/2N2N.text:
And we play d6, controlling e5.

In the resulting position we'll have ideas of trading the c3-knight for our knight after jumping to e4, developing the knight to d7 and our queen to e7.

rn1q1rk1/pbpp2bp/1p2pnp1/3P1p2/2P5/P1N2N.text:
And now the advance to d5 is played. After this point you'll notice that the c5 square has been given up by White.

So let's develop a piece with the idea of jumping to c5 at some point.

rn1q1rk1/pbpp2bp/1p2pnp1/3P1pB1/2P5/2N2N.text:
This move is almost always possible.

Let's just jump to a6, looking at the c5 square.

rn1q1rk1/pbpp2bp/1p2pnp1/5p2/2PP1B2/2N2N.text: White forms the battery with the queen and bishop.

rn1q1rk1/pbpp2bp/1p2pnp1/5pB1/2PP4/2N2NP.text:
White forms a bishop and queen battery, maybe with the idea of trading our good bishop on g7 via Bh6.

Let's get the queen out of the pin.

rn1qk2r/pbpp2bp/1p2Pnp1/5p2/2P5/5NP1/PP2.text:
White can opt for the very natural capture here.

We will recapture.

rn1qk2r/pbpp2bp/1p2pnp1/3P1p2/2P5/2N2NP1.text:
This move gains space for White, and blocks off our bishop on b7.

In reply we will take advantage of the recently made available c5 square by playing ...Na6.

rn1qk2r/pbpp2bp/1p2pnp1/5p2/2PP1B2/2N2NP.text:
White continues developing their forces.

In reply we can simply castle.

rn1qk2r/pbpp2bp/1p2pnp1/5p2/2PP4/P1N2NP1.text:
White castles.

Black castles as well.

rn1qk2r/pbpp2bp/1p2pnp1/5pB1/2PP4/2N2NP1.text:
This pins our knight to the queen.

Let's just castle and give our knight another defender.

rn1qkb1r/pbpp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/2PP4/5NP1/PP.text:
White castles. And here very important: anticipating that White may end up going d5, we can choose to fianchetto our dark-squared bishop, which in turn will control many dark squares running along the a1-h8 diagonal.

Thus we continue with ...g6.

rn1qkb1r/pbpp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/2PP4/P4NP1/1.text:
After Bg2 entering the coveted diagonal, I suggest a double bishop fianchetto system.

We will play g6.

rn1qkb1r/pbpp3p/1p2pnp1/3P1p2/2P5/5NP1/P.text:
White can also decide to push now.

We can now enter the diagonal weakened by the d5 push.

rn1qkb1r/pbpp3p/1p2pnp1/5p2/2PP4/2N2NP1/.text:
White can continue with normal development by playing their knight to c3.

We will occupy the long diagonal.

rn1qkb1r/pbpp3p/1p2pnp1/5p2/2PP4/P1N2NP1.text:
White develops normally.

And we fulfill our idea of bringing the bishop to g7.

rn1qkbnr/pbpp1ppp/1p2p3/8/2PP4/5NP1/PP2P.text:
White chooses to enter the h1-a8 diagonal.

Here we can in reply push f5 and control e4 further.

rn1qkbnr/pbpp1ppp/1p2p3/8/2PP4/P4N2/1P2P.text:
This move order prevents us from developing to b4.

After 4.a3 we can respond with f5 to control the e4 square, as we have already done throughout this course.

rn1qkbnr/pbpp2pp/1p2p3/5p2/2PP4/5NP1/PP2.text:
White gets to the desired diagonal.

And we continue development with an eye to e4.

rn1qkbnr/pbpp2pp/1p2p3/5p2/2PP4/P4NP1/1P.text:
White plays g3 to enter the diagonal themselves.

But we develop, further controlling e4.

rn1qkbnr/pbpppppp/1p6/8/2PP4/5N2/PP2PPPP.text:
White brings the knight out, blocking our bishop's diagonal. Taking the knight with 3...Bxf3 makes little sense here, as White could then capture towards the center with 4. gxf3, followed by playing e4, and they'd have a powerful center. 

Let's continue with e6, with the idea of playing Bb4 should White choose to bring a knight to c3.

rn2qrk1/p1pp2bp/1p2p1p1/5pB1/2PPb3/5NP1/.text:
And we just recapture with our bishop.

Very natural developing moves will follow. The move ...d6 will be played to cover some central squares.

We can expect Bh6 from White, to trade off the dark-squared bishops. In that case, we can simply trade and bring our queen to e7.

rn2qrk1/pbpp2bp/1p2pnp1/5pB1/2PP4/2N2NP1.text:
White adds another piece to the d-file.

Now we can jump to e4, attacking the queen and thus we'll probably achieve a trade, which is good when we have less space in a position.

rnbqkbnr/p1pppppp/1p6/8/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
White plays c4, controlling the central d5 square from the side. d5 is an important square in these variations, so pay close attention to the play surrounding it.

Let's fianchetto the bishop with an eye on g2.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
Welcome to the chapter on countering the Catalan. In this study, you'll learn some strategies when white chooses to go on the h1-a8 diagonal after 1.d4 b6 2.c4 Bb7 3.Nf3 e6 and either g3 or a3 on move 4. 

First, let's prepare the fianchetto.

rnk1r3/pbp3bp/1p2pnp1/5p2/2P2B2/2N2NP1/P.text:
White develops looking at c7 which is defended by our king.

We continue with development. We realize that if White plays Nb5 the d7-knight supports an e5 pawn push, blocking the f4-bishop.

rnk4r/pbp3bp/1p2pnp1/5p2/2P5/2N2NP1/PP2P.text:
White continues with regular development.

Let's bring a rook in to defend our weakest link in the position.

r2q1rk1/pb1p2pp/1pnppn2/5p2/3P4/2PBPN2/P.text:
White's idea here is to push e4.

And now we allow White to play e4 if and only if they want massive trades in the center!

r2q1rk1/pb1pn1pp/1p1pp3/8/3PB3/2P2N2/PP3.text:
They recapture.

And we will exchange bishops.

r2q1rk1/pb1pn1pp/1p1ppn2/8/3PN3/2PB1N2/P.text: They recapture. But we can trade both minor pieces off.

r2q1rk1/pbpp2pp/1p1bp3/3nNp1n/3P4/2PBPNB.text: We insist on getting that bishop! Maybe White should have just traded on d6 earlier!

r2q1rk1/pbpp2pp/1p2p3/3nPp2/3P4/2PB2P1/P.text:
Once they do this...

Qg5 threatens f4, which is better for Black.

r2q1rk1/pbpp2pp/1pn1p3/3nNp2/3P1P2/2PB2P.text:
Suppose White guards f4 by playing g3...

We can trade and tempt White to undouble their pawns.

r2q1rk1/pbpp2pp/1pn1pn2/4Np2/3P1P2/2PB4/.text:
Ne5 is not a surprise at all.

But we can jump into the center too and attack f4.

r2q1rk1/pbpp2pp/1pnbpn2/4Np2/3P1B2/2PBPN.text:
Instead, they often support their knight with the other knight.

But we're maneuvering to d5 to harass the bishop!

r2q1rk1/pbppn1pp/1p1bpn2/4Np2/3P1B2/2PBP.text:
For example, White may well develop their queen...

We will go after the bishop pair.

r4rk1/p1qpn1pp/1p1pp3/8/3PR3/2P2N2/PP3PP.text: It's hard to see how White's going to win, and our rook is placed on the semi-open f-file!

r4rk1/pbpp2pp/1p2p3/3nPp1q/3P4/2PB1NP1/P.text:
Our queen stays lurking in the kingside, where it threatens to continue the assault on White's position. 

We have an excellent position, as the light squares in front of the White king are weak.

r4rk1/pbpp2pp/1p2p3/3nPpq1/3P4/2PB1NP1/P.text: And if White doesn't play f4 themselves...

rn1q1rk1/pb1p2pp/1p1ppn2/5p2/3P4/2PBPN2/.text:
White achieves their London structure.

We develop the knight to c6. It often travels to e7.

rn1q1rk1/pbp1b1pp/1p2p3/3p1p2/3PnB2/2PBP.text: And we cement our knight on e4. We've also got ideas of g5 at some point!

rn1q1rk1/pbpp2pp/1p1bpn2/4Np2/3P1B2/2PBP.text:
White achieves their London pawn structure.

We will propose a knight trade with ...Nc6. White probably won't take.

rn1q1rk1/pbpp2pp/1p1bpn2/5p2/3P4/2PBPNB1.text:
If they play a useful waiting move like c3...

Exchanging is actually quite safe.

rn1q1rk1/pbpp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/3P1P2/2PB1N2.text:
And so does White.

We will develop our knight.

rn1q1rk1/pbpp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/3P4/2PBPNP1/.text:
Because even though the rook gets a semi-open file...

If we can control the queen's entry square, we have a safe position.

rn1q1rk1/pbppb1pp/1p2p3/5p2/3PnB2/2PBPN2.text: White gets the traditional triangle pawn structure of the London.

rn1qk2r/pb1p2pp/1p1ppn2/5p2/3P4/3BPN2/PP.text:
White castles...

And so do we.

rn1qk2r/pbpp2pp/1p1Bpn2/5p2/3P4/3BPN2/PP.text:
This is another rational response. Maybe White thinks that doubling our pawns is bad. On the contrary, another central pawn can be very useful!

We recapture. Our extra d-pawn helps control the e5 square! White won't get their usual Ne5 play!

rn1qk2r/pbpp2pp/1p1bpn2/4Np2/3P1B2/3BP3/.text:
White could stay true to London style of play, and thus they jump the knight to e5.

Let's just castle. The knight might look good on e5, but it isn't harming us in any way.

rn1qk2r/pbpp2pp/1p1bpn2/5p2/3P1B2/2PBPN2.text:
This is one of White's rarer responses. It simply chooses to do nothing about the tension between the bishops. White is figuring that moving their bishop loses tempo. 

We will swap on f4 and double White's pawns.

rn1qk2r/pbpp2pp/1p1bpn2/5p2/3P4/3BPNB1/P.text:
This is White's most popular response. It's actually a knee-jerk reaction from many London players. They don't tend to trade, but many just go back to g3 so they can trade on their terms.

We'll simply castle.

rn1qk2r/pbpp2pp/1p1bpn2/5pB1/3P4/3BPN2/P.text:
White chooses to reject the trade and they pin us instead.

We unpin with ...Be7. A future Ne4 will revive the idea of trading.

rn1qk2r/pbppB1pp/1p2p3/5p2/3Pn3/3BPN2/PP.text:
White could accept the trade.

We recapture.

rn1qk2r/pbppb1pp/1p2p3/5p2/3PnB2/3BPN2/P.text:
Maybe White elects to keep the bishop on.

We will go ahead and castle.

rn1qk2r/pbppb1pp/1p2pn2/5pB1/3P4/3BPN2/P.text:
White castles.

We insist on trying to trade pieces off.

rn1qkb1r/pbpp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/3P1B2/3BPN2/.text:
White develops to d2, as is done in the London. White plans to play a pawn to c3.

Our idea is to immediately challenge the dark-squared bishop with Bd6. This is one of White's best pieces. If we trade it, there will be less pressure on our position.

rn1qkbnr/pbpp1ppp/1p2p3/8/3P1B2/4PN2/PPP.text:
White continues and supports d4 and f4.

We will play f5, controlling e4 from the side.
White develops to f3 in true London-style.

rn1qkbnr/pbpp2pp/1p2p3/5p2/3P1B2/3BPN2/P.text:
White develops, looking at the e4 square.

We develop our knight, fighting for more control of e4.

rn1qkbnr/pbpp2pp/1p2p3/5p2/3P1B2/4PN2/PP.text: And we play f5, controlling e4. As you can see, White might alter the move order, but our moves remain the same.

rn1qkbnr/pbpppppp/1p6/8/3P1B2/4P3/PPP2PP.text:
Should White go e3 first, do not dismay. It's just a slightly different move order.

Our third move is still e6.

rn1qkbnr/pbpppppp/1p6/8/3P1B2/5N2/PPP1PP.text:
White develops the knight in typical London fashion.

We will open up our bishop and control some central light squares.

rn2k2r/pbppq1pp/1p2p3/4Np2/3Pn3/3BP3/PPP.text:
Ne5 is to be expected in the London.

Simply react to it normally. Castling is always useful.

rn2qrk1/p1p3pp/1p2pn2/3p2N1/3Pp3/2P1P1P1.text:
We can just push and consolidate our structure, and the e-pawn is defended by the queen.

White's knight is a bit stranded on the g-file, and they'll have to think of ways to relocate it.

rn2qrk1/p1pp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/3PB3/2P1PNP1/.text:
So if White trades bishops...

We recapture with the pawn.

rn2qrk1/p1pp2pp/1p2pn2/6N1/3Pp3/2P1P1P1/.text: The knight jumps forward and attacks e4.

rn2qrk1/pbpp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/3P4/2PBPNP1/P.text:
That's why if White attemps to play e4 to get some more squares for their pieces...

We put our bishop on e4. A trade on this square will close the position in our favor, and White's queen will be limited to the light squares.

rn3rk1/pbp1q1pp/1p1ppn2/5p2/2NP4/3BPP2/P.text:
It goes to the only square available.

Now g6 supports the f-pawn in case of e4.

rn3rk1/pbp1q2p/1p1pp1p1/5p1n/2NPP3/3B1P2.text: And additionally we can threaten to fork White! We're basically in the middle game, and White hasn't achieved any advantage!

rn3rk1/pbp1q2p/1p1ppnp1/5p2/2NPP3/3B1P2/.text: So after White's break on e4, attacking our f-pawn, we now have a defender in the form of the g6 pawn.

rn3rk1/pbppq1pp/1p2p3/4Np2/3Pn3/3BPP2/PP.text:
The position of our knight is very strong on e4. That's why White may try to kick it out.

We go back, but now we're threatening to expel the strong e5-knight.

rn3rk1/pbppq1pp/1p2pn2/4Np2/3P4/3BPP2/PP.text:
White connects their rooks.

We will play ...d6 and kick the knight out.

rnbqkbnr/p1pppppp/1p6/8/3P1B2/8/PPP1PPPP.text:
And now this is the clear indication that White will go for the London.

We will simply fianchetto.

rnbqkbnr/p1pppppp/1p6/8/3P4/5N2/PPP1PPPP.text:
Alternatively, White could bring out the knight first. In which case, they could still be going for a London setup, as after we develop, they'd play Bf4.

We fianchetto.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
Welcome to the chapter on the London. What to do when white goes for the very common and solid London setup? Well, we have our repertoire of strategies, going for a fianchetto of our bishop, controlling e4 via f5 and proposing an early trade on d6!

Let's prepare to fianchetto as normal.

r2q1rk1/1bpnnppp/1p1p4/p3p3/P1P1P3/2PP1N.text:
You know the drill! Stop White from gaining space on the queenside and place another pawn on a dark square. Seems like win-win for us.

We might expect moves like d4 and Nh4 from White. In that case, we can counter-attack with ...f5!

r2q1rk1/pbpnnppp/1p1p4/4p3/P1P1P3/2PP1NP.text: White attempts to gain space on the queenside.

r2q1rk1/pbpnnppp/1p1pp3/8/2P1P3/2PP1NP1/.text:
White places the rook on a more active square.

And yet another pawn in the dark-square complex. A sound strategy like Capablanca and Nimzowitsch used to employ.

rn1q1rk1/pbp1nppp/1p1pp3/8/2P1P3/2PP1NP1.text:
White pushes and gains space with e4.

d6 also freed a square for our knight to develop to, and we'll place our knight on d7.

rn1q1rk1/pbppnppp/1p2p3/8/2P5/2PP1NP1/P3.text:
d3 defends c4. You'll notice no pawn can now defend the backwards c3 pawn.

We play the sound d6, placing our pawns on the dark-square complex since we have parted with our dark-square bishop.

rn1qk1nr/pbpp1ppp/1p2p3/8/1bP5/2N2NP1/PP.text: If White develops in this standard way, we feel free to capture on c3.

rn1qk1nr/pbpp1ppp/1p2p3/8/2P5/2P2NP1/P2P.text:
White recaptures towards the center.

We will continue with normal development, placing our knight on e7.

rn1qk2r/pbppnppp/1p2p3/8/2P5/2P2NP1/P2PP.text:
White castles.

And so do we.

rn1qkbnr/pbpp1ppp/1p2p3/8/2P5/2N2NP1/PP1.text:
White can decide they want to join the powerful h1-a8 diagonal as well, since right now we occupy it unopposed.

In this course we'll recommend ...Bb4, with the idea of damaging White's pawns, and removing a piece that controls d5 and e4.

rn1qkbnr/pbpppppp/1p6/8/2P5/2N2N2/PP1PPP.text:
White develops the knight where it controls the most central squares. Additionally, they block off the diagonal from our bishop.

In reply, we will play e6, preparing to strike in the central light squares and opening the diagonal of our dark-squared bishop.

rnbqkbnr/p1pppppp/1p6/8/2P5/2N5/PP1PPPPP.text:
White develops a knight, which is poised to control d5 as well.

We now enter the diagonal with our fianchettoed bishop.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/2P5/8/PP1PPPPP/RNB.text:
Welcome to the chapter on beating the English. In this study, we'll begin by looking at how to play against White's very common setup fianchettoing the light-squared bishop in the English structure. We'll also introduce the Black player to some of the intricacies of playing against the English.

We begin our development with b6, like in the previous d4 chapters.

r2q1rk1/p1pp2pp/bp4n1/n2P1p2/2P5/2PB1N2/.text:
White doubles major pieces on the e-file.

But we can propose a trade by gaining a tempo on the queen. This would be advantageous as c4 is weak, and becomes weaker the more pieces we can exchange.

r2q1rk1/p1ppn1pp/bp2p3/n2P1p2/2P1P3/2PB1.text:
White defends the c4-pawn.

We'll capture on d5.

r2q1rk1/p1ppn1pp/bp6/n2P1p2/2P5/2PB1N2/P.text:
White recaptures, opening a line to f5. At the moment, though, they are busy defending c4.

We can bring our knight to a more active square, covering a potential e5 invasion from the f3-knight.

r2q1rk1/pbppn1pp/1p2p3/n2P1p2/2P1P3/2P2N.text:
White gains space.

We'll strike at c4 with ...Ba6.

r2q1rk1/pbppn1pp/1pn1p3/5p2/1bPPP3/2N2N2.text:
White pushes d4, gaining space!

We capture on c3, damaging the pawns, and undermining e4.

r2q1rk1/pbppn1pp/1pn1p3/5p2/2PPP3/2P2N2/.text:
White recaptures towards the center.

With ...Na5, we open up our bishop, apply pressure on c4 with the knight, and pressure on e4 with the bishop.

r2q2k1/p1pp2pp/bp4n1/n2P1p2/2P5/2PB4/P1Q.text:
White recaptures the only way possible.

We gain control of the e-file with tempo, hitting the knight on e1.

r2qk1nr/p1pp1ppp/1pn1p3/4P3/1bP5/2N3Q1/P.text:
White here defends e5 and attacks g7, but...

We will play enterprisingly. We offer the g-pawn, with ideas of gaining tempi on the queen, and maybe even trapping her.

r2qk1nr/p1pp2pp/1pn1P3/8/1bP5/2N2P2/PPQP.text:
White can greedily snatch another pawn...

And we can develop yet another piece!

r2qk2r/p1pp1pQp/1pn1p1n1/4P3/1bP4P/2N5/P.text:
White can push the pawn, with the idea of removing the defender of h8.

But we can recapture our pawn safely, because we have a nice trick up our sleeve.

r2qk2r/p1ppnpQp/1pn1p3/4P3/1bP5/2N5/PP1P.text:
White takes, and hits the rook.

Here we defend the rook, and limit the mobility of the queen. We're also attacking e5 twice.

r2qkb1r/p1pp1pQp/1p2p1n1/4n2P/2P5/2N5/PP.text: We don't have to move the knight. The queen is trapped!

r2qr1k1/p1pp2pp/bp4n1/n2P1p2/2P5/2PB1N2/.text:
White chooses to keep the queen on the board. 

We will still swap rooks, though.

r3k2r/p1pq2pp/1pn2n2/8/1bP5/2N2P2/PPQP1P.text: But then we end up with four developed pieces and a castled king, before White even finds a home for their king.

r3q1k1/p1pp2pp/1p4n1/n2P1BB1/2b5/2P5/P1Q.text: White can grab our f-pawn, but...

r3q1k1/p1pp2pp/1p4n1/n2b1BB1/8/2P5/P1Q2P.text:
We can also gobble up the remains of their center!

Our plan is to make room for our rook with ...Qf7, after which we can retreat the bishop to b7 or improve our knight via c4.

r3q1k1/p1pp2pp/bp4n1/n2P1pB1/2P5/2PB4/P1.text:
White develops a bishop and defends e1 with the rook.

But now we can take on c4.

rn1q1rk1/pbp1nppp/1p1pp3/8/2P1P3/P1PB1N2.text: And we play d6, holding off on concrete central play, but placing a pawn on a dark-square since we have parted ways with our dark-squared bishop.

rn1q1rk1/pbpp2pp/1p2p1n1/4Pp2/1bP5/2NP1N.text: But we can increase the pressure with our knight moving to g6.

rn1q1rk1/pbppn1pp/1p2p3/4Pp2/1bP5/2NP1N2.text: White can try to avoid our aggressive intentions and keep lines closed by playing e5.

rn1q1rk1/pbppn1pp/1p2p3/5p2/1bP1P3/2N2N2.text:
White can ignore this push and simply develop their queen.

We'll develop to c6.

rn1q1rk1/pbppnppp/1p2p3/8/1bP1P3/2N2N2/P.text:
White frees the way for the d-pawn.

Here we can strike in the center! If exf5, our bishop will look at f3 and our rook will exert pressure down the f-file.

rn1q1rk1/pbppnppp/1p2p3/8/1bP1P3/2NP1N2/.text:
And so does White.

Now we will play energetically, and strike out at the white center with ...f5.

rn1qk1nr/p1pp1ppp/1p2p3/4P3/1bP5/2N2Q2/P.text:
White recaptures with a queen, gaining a tempo on our rook.

But we block the diagonal and gain a tempo on e5 while also controlling d4.

rn1qk1nr/p1pp2pp/1p2p3/5P2/1bP5/2N2P2/PP.text:
White recaptures.

Quick development is key! We'll bring our queen's knight out.

rn1qk1nr/pbpp1ppp/1p2p3/4P3/1bP5/2N2N2/P.text:
Finally, White can see they're under attack on e4 so they can push the pawn up one square, with the idea of gaining control of f6 and d6.

We'll capture on f3, arguing that the removal of the supporting knight renders the white center over-extended.

rn1qk1nr/pbpp1ppp/1p2p3/8/1bP1P3/2N2N2/P.text:
White can also try Qc2, defending e4.

Let's undermine the center in a provocative way, with ...f5!

rn1qk1nr/pbpp1ppp/1p2p3/8/1bP1P3/2NB1N2/.text:
White can continue with this move, which defends the e4-pawn after a potential bishop capture on c3.

We'll just continue with normal development, and bring the knight to e7.

rn1qk1nr/pbpp1ppp/1p2p3/8/1bP1P3/2NP1N2/.text:
White can also defend e4 with a pawn.

Developing the knight with ...Ne7 is a good idea.

rn1qk1nr/pbpp2pp/1p2p3/5P2/1bP5/2N2N2/PP.text:
White captures.

We'll take on f3, damaging the pawns.

rn1qk2r/pbppnppp/1p2p3/8/1bP1P3/2NB1N2/P.text:
White gets their king into safety.

We'll do likewise.

rn1qk2r/pbppnppp/1p2p3/8/1bP1P3/2NP1N2/P.text:
White prepares to castle.

We will castle.

rn1qk2r/pbppnppp/1p2p3/8/1bP1P3/P1NB1N2/.text:
If White attacks us on b4...

We'll capture and damage their pawn structure.

rn1qk2r/pbppnppp/1p2p3/8/2P1P3/P1PB1N2/1.text:
White recaptures away from the center, giving their queen some scope, and giving the c1-bishop a diagonal to work with.

We'll castle into safety.

rn1qkbnr/pbpp1ppp/1p2p3/8/2P1P3/2N2N2/PP.text:
White develops, controlling central squares.

After our reply of ...Bb4, we threaten to take on c3, double the pawns, and win e4 in the process!

rn1qkbnr/pbpppppp/1p6/8/2P1P3/2N5/PP1P1P.text:
White's knight sufficiently defends e4, so White stakes a claim to the center.

Let's prepare to bring our bishop out with ...e6.

rnbqkbnr/p1pppppp/1p6/8/2P5/2N5/PP1PPPPP.text:
White develops, controlling central squares.

We'll get our bishop onto the effective a8-h1 diagonal.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/2P5/8/PP1PPPPP/RNB.text:
Welcome to the final study of this chapter! You'll learn how to combat a very common setup White can go for in the English. After 1.c4 b6 2.Nc3 Bb7 3.e4 e6 4.Nf3 Bb4 - you can refer to this as the Two Knights in the English by White.

We will prepare to fianchetto our bishop.

lessons.title: The Reti with a Queenside Fianchetto

r2q1rk1/1bppb1pp/np2pn2/p4p2/4P3/1P1P1NP.text:
White achieves e4!

We will take a central pawn with our f-pawn.

r3qrk1/1bppb1pp/np2pn2/p7/4P3/1P3NP1/PBP.text:
The queen has good play on the light squares.

White has achieved their central pawn break, but on the other hand our rook is now well-placed on the half-open f-file.

rn1q1rk1/1bppb1pp/1p2pn2/p4p2/8/1P1P1NP1.text:
Again with the idea of supporting e2-e4.

We can develop our knight without blocking off our bishop.

rn1q1rk1/pbp1bppp/1p3n2/3p4/8/1P3NP1/PB1.text:
And we castle, too.

We have good control over the e4-square: the knight might end up there in the future.

Simple moves like ...Nbd7 developing and ...c6 supporting the center are useful to us.

rn1q1rk1/pbpp2bp/1p2pnp1/5p2/2PP4/1P2PN2.text:
We simply castle. 

We have a nice grip over the e4 square.

The main plan is to bring the queen to e7, push ...d6, develop the knight and later even go for a ...c5 push.

rn1q1rk1/pbppb1pp/1p2pn2/5p2/8/1P1P1NP1/.text:
White develops another piece, again supporting the central break with a future e4.

We can expand on the queenside!

rn1qk2r/pbpp2bp/1p2pnp1/5p2/2PP4/1P2PN2/.text: White proceeds with c4, fighting for control of d5.

rn1qk2r/pbppb1pp/1p2pn2/5p2/8/1P1P1NP1/P.text:
White might attempt to prepare an e4 push.

Meanwhile, we're going to bring our king into safety.

rn1qkb1r/pbp2ppp/1p2pn2/3P4/8/1P3NP1/PB1.text:
White may capture our center pawn.

We will recapture with the e-pawn.

rn1qkb1r/pbp2ppp/1p3n2/3p4/8/1P3NP1/PB1P.text:
White fianchettoes.

Here we will bring our bishop out.

rn1qkb1r/pbpp1ppp/1p2pn2/8/2P5/1P3NP1/PB.text:
If White goes for a double fianchetto...

We can strike in the center with d5!

rn1qkb1r/pbpp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/8/1P2PN2/PBP.text:
White castles.

Here we can go for the double fianchetto.

rn1qkb1r/pbpp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/8/1P3NP1/PBP.text:
White castles.

We will develop the bishop and support the knight on f6.

rn1qkb1r/pbpp3p/1p2pnp1/5p2/3P4/1P2PN2/P.text:
White gains space in the center.

We fianchetto.

rn1qkbnr/pbpp1ppp/1p2p3/8/2P5/1P3N2/PB1P.text:
Finally c4 is suggested by the engine, and it's played by some people. The idea is to fight for control of d5.

We can develop and block the bishop's sight down the long diagonal.

rn1qkbnr/pbpp1ppp/1p2p3/8/8/1P2PN2/PBPP1.text:
By far the most popular move in this position. It opens up the light-squared bishop.

Let's go f5 and control e4!

rn1qkbnr/pbpp1ppp/1p2p3/8/8/1P3NP1/PBPPP.text:
This move indicates that White wants to go for the double fianchetto! A true hyper-modern way of playing!

Here we can preface Nf6 blocking the diagonal with the pawn push ...f5. We are playing to control e4.

rn1qkbnr/pbpp2pp/1p2p3/5p2/8/1P2PN2/PBPP.text:
White continues to develop, preparing castling.

Let's block off the bishop's view of g7.

rn1qkbnr/pbpp2pp/1p2p3/5p2/8/1P3NP1/PBPP.text:
White will fianchetto.

And we will play the knight to f6, blocking off the b2-bishop slightly.

rn1qkbnr/pbpppppp/1p6/8/8/1P3N2/PBPPPPPP.text:
White controls their diagonal too.

We play e6, getting ready for a potential d5 or f5 pawn push. Here White has many moves available to choose from. We'll go over the most popular ones.

Don't move your bishop on f8 until you block off the white's bishop's access to g7!

rnbqkbnr/p1pppppp/1p6/8/8/1P3N2/P1PPPPPP.text:
b3, with the idea of a fianchetto to control the a1-h8 diagonal.

We fianchetto, stepping into the a8-h1 diagonal.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/5N2/PPPPPPPP/RNB.text:
Welcome to the ninth chapter! Congratulations on making it this far. This chapter will answer the questions: what if White doesn't open with e4/d4/c4, which are the most popular options? What if White chooses a hyper-modern setup with 1.Nf3? 

The convenient thing about our system is that our moves remain good and easy to remember. We will play 1...b6, once again preparing to fianchetto.

lessons.title: The Reti with a Kingside Fianchetto

r2q1rk1/pbp1b1pp/1pn1p3/3p4/8/2NP2P1/PPP.text:
White is obliged to return to c3, where the bishop would have liked to go.

We will place the queen on d7, defending our backwards e6 pawn and preparing to connect the rooks.

r2q1rk1/pbpp2p1/1pn1p2p/7Q/4N3/2PP2P1/P1.text:
Thus we here block the diagonal and protect against the discovery.

We can reroute the knight to f5 and play ...Qe7 to connect the rooks!

r2q1rk1/pbpp2pp/1pn1pb2/8/4N3/3P2P1/PPP2.text:
White brings the knight into the center, threatening to grab the bishop pair in an open position.

We will preserve our bishop.

r2q1rk1/pbppb1pp/1pn1p3/8/4N3/3P2P1/PPPB.text:
White develops the bishop, probably with the idea of activating it on c3.

We can expand and gain a tempo on the knight!

r2q1rk1/pbppb1pp/1pn1pN2/8/8/2NP2P1/PPP2.text:
White opts to exchange knights, figuring the c3-knight can replace the other knight by hopping to e4 itself. 

We will take back on f6 with the bishop.

r2qk2r/pbp3p1/1pnppn1p/2b5/4PP2/6PN/PPP3.text: The move d6 applies some control to e5, and can be played as our bishop isn't behind the pawns anymore. Play will continue by securing the bishop on c5 via a7-a5, and castling.

r2qk2r/pbpp2p1/1pn1pn1p/2b5/4PP2/6PN/PPP.text: The knight retreats to h3. White needs to maintain the defense of  the e4-pawn with the bishop.

r2qk2r/pbpp2pp/1pn1pn2/2b3N1/4PP2/6P1/PP.text:
The king moves.

We will push the g5-knight back. Perhaps White should have just centralized their knight by capturing on e4.

r2qk2r/pbpp2pp/1pnbpn2/6N1/4PP2/6P1/PPP3.text:
f4 might be played here, with the idea of going e5 and forking knight and bishop.

We'll simply sidestep with check. Maybe White will later find that f4 has weakened their king position.

r2qk2r/pbppb1pp/1pn1pn2/8/4N3/2NP2P1/PPP.text:
White develops a knight, protecting its comrade on e4.

We will castle into safety.

r2qkb1r/pbpp2pp/1pn1pn2/6N1/4P3/6P1/PPP2.text:
This move, on the other hand, seeks to maintain an e-pawn in the center.

We can develop our bishop on d6, preventing an e5 push.

r2qkb1r/pbpp2pp/1pn1pn2/8/4N3/3P2P1/PPP2.text:
This move centralizes the knight.

We will just develop a piece and get closer to castling.

r4rk1/pbpqb1pp/1p2p3/3pn3/6Q1/2NP2P1/PPP.text: So let's allow our bishop to defend d5 as well, while gaining a tempo on the queen, with the idea of later settling our knight on g6!

r4rk1/pbpqb1pp/1pn1p3/3p4/6Q1/2NP2P1/PPP.text: White develops the queen. This is a tricky move, threatening to capture on d5 thanks to the pin on the e-pawn.

rn1q1rk1/pbpp2p1/1p2p2p/3n3Q/4N3/2BP2P1/.text:
Qg6, threatening checkmate on h7 and g7 simultaneously, doesn't work, as we have Qxg5, removing the threat of mate on h7 and defending g7 with the queen.

Therefore White recaptures the pawn, getting the knight out of danger.

Let's eliminate the strong c3-bishop!

rn1q1rk1/pbpp2p1/1p2p2p/7Q/4N3/2PP2P1/P1.text: White recaptures with the b-pawn. This threatens a Nf6+ discovery, which would win our b7-bishop and then the rook behind it on a8.

rn1q1rk1/pbpp2pp/1p2p3/3n2NQ/4p3/2BP2P1/.text:
Checkmate its threatened! We need to deal with that before proceeding.

We will attack the knight and block the checkmate threat. This forces White to move away with the knight.

rn1q1rk1/pbpp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/1b2P3/2NP1NP.text:
White strikes with e4!

Let's remove the knight supporting  e4.

rn1q1rk1/pbpp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/4P3/2BP1NP1/.text:
White recaptures with the bishop to preserve the integrity of their pawn structure.

We take on e4, as this is better for us, structurally speaking.

rn1q1rk1/pbpp2pp/1p2pn2/6N1/4p3/2BP2P1/P.text:
The correct move for White. Our pawn is pinned to our bishop!

With ...Nd5 we attack the bishop, but also we block off the long diagonal and revive capturing on d3 as a threat.

rn1qk2r/pbpp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/1b6/2NP1NP1/P.text:
White defends c3 to recapture with their bishop should we take.

We will get our king into safety.

rn1qkb1r/pbpp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/4P3/3P1NP1/P.text:
White pushes e4. It is supported tactically, as we will see!

Let's make use of our f-pawn by capturing a central pawn.

rn1qkb1r/pbpp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/8/2NP1NP1/PP.text:
White may choose to prepare e4 with the knight, in which case...

We get ready to trade our bishop for the knight and remove the supporter of e4.

rn1qkb1r/pbpp2pp/1p2pn2/6N1/4p3/3P2P1/PP.text:
This pins and attacks our pawn, with the idea of recapturing on e4.

Let's just develop. We can't stop White regaining their pawn.

rn1qkbnr/pbpp1ppp/1p2p3/8/8/5NP1/PPPPPPB.text:
White castles their king into safety. This defends the bishop on g2. Beware of any discoveries by the knight!

We will go f5, controlling e4. If White plays d4 or c4, we'll be in familiar territory.

rn1qkbnr/pbpp2pp/1p2p3/5p2/8/3P1NP1/PPP1.text:
White can choose to continue this way, preparing an e2-e4 push.

We develop, fighting for control of e4.

rn1qkbnr/pbpppppp/1p6/8/8/5NP1/PPPPPPBP/.text:
White fianchettoes.

We prepare to bring out our other bishop.

rnbqkbnr/p1pppppp/1p6/8/8/5NP1/PPPPPP1P/.text:
White intends to go on the same diagonal we're going. Copycat!

We'll get there first!

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/5N2/PPPPPPPP/RNB.text:
Welcome to the second and final study of this chapter. Here, you'll learn how to combat White's setup should they go for 1.Nf3 b6 2.g3, to fianchetto their bishop on the a8-h1 diagonal. 

This is the same diagonal we're fianchettoed in, so stick around because White might also choose a double fianchetto in a true hyper-modern sense!

Here we will employ our by now familiar strategy, the fianchetto.

lessons.title: White Plays g3/b3/Nc3/e3 on Move 1 - Preparing against the 400s

r1b1r1k1/1pq2pp1/2pb1n1p/2n1p3/P3P3/2P2N.text: And this knight jump places pressure on both e4 and a4, while reaching a square from which no pawn can remove it. Additionally, e6 will be a good square to develop the c8-bishop.

r1b1r1k1/1pqn1pp1/2pb1n1p/3pp3/P3P3/2PP1.text: If White takes it, temporarily gaining a pawn, we will exchange in the center.

r1b1r1k1/1pqn1pp1/2pb1n1p/p2pp3/4P3/1PPP.text:
A queenside fianchetto.

We'll expand on the queenside.

r1bqk1nr/ppp2ppp/2n5/2b1p3/2Pp4/3P1NP1/P.text:
White can castle.

Now that our bishop is out we will develop the knight to e7.

r1bqk2r/1pp1nppp/2n5/p1b1p3/2Pp4/P2P1NP1.text: We can play a5 to counter this advance and to give our bishop retreating options. We'll be able to proceed with castling and getting our king to safety.

r1bqk2r/ppp1nppp/2n5/2b1p3/2Pp4/P2P1NP1/.text: White can play a3, with the idea of harassing our queenside pieces and gaining space.

r1bqkbnr/ppp2ppp/2n5/4p3/2Pp4/3P1NP1/PP2.text:
White can develop pressurizing our center. 

We'll develop our bishop to c5 to make an e3 pawn break tougher to play.

r1bqr1k1/1p1n1pp1/2pb1n1p/p2pp3/4P3/1PPP.text:
Giving the bishop scope to develop on b2.

We can develop the queen, further supporting our pawn center.

r1bqr1k1/1p1n1ppp/2pb1n2/p2pp3/4P3/2PP1N.text:
White develops their queen.

...h6 is a useful move for us here, preventing a minor piece from ever landing on g5.

r1bqr1k1/pp1n1ppp/2pb1n2/3pp3/4P3/2PP1NP.text:
c3 is a popular move, White fights for control of d4 and maybe contemplates developing the queen on c2.

We can begin a middle game plan of gaining space in the queenside. We're not really aiming to attack on the kingside any time soon, so queenside play it is.

rn1q1rk1/pbpp2bp/1p2pnp1/5p2/3P4/1P1BPN2.text:
And we castle as well.

As before, ...Qe7, ...d6, ...c5 — all of these moves are very natural in this position.

rn1q1rk1/pbppb1pp/1p2p3/5p2/2PPn3/1PN1PN.text:
We jump our knight into the center.

This is the end! Congratulations! Study the rest of the chapters, and keep this one in mind in case your opponents lash out with these rare options!

rn1q1rk1/pbppb1pp/1p2pn2/5p2/2PP4/1PN1PN.text: White prepares to develop the bishop on b2.

rn1qk2r/pbpp1ppp/1p2pn2/8/1b1PP3/2NB1N2/.text: Meanwhile, we can continue piling up on e4 like in previous chapters.

rn1qk2r/pbpp2bp/1p2pnp1/5p2/3P4/1P1BPN2/.text: White castles to get their king into safety.

rn1qk2r/pbppb1pp/1p2pn2/5p2/2PP4/2N1PN2/.text:
White brings their knight out after pushing c4.

And we can get our king to safety.

rn1qkb1r/pbpp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/2PP4/4PN2/PP.text:
After c4 gaining space for White...

We will develop, getting ready to castle.

rn1qkb1r/pbpp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/3P4/1P2PN2/P.text:
White supports d4 and gives their light-squared bishop scope to develop.

The double fianchetto is our idea here.

rn1qkb1r/pbpp3p/1p2pnp1/5p2/3P4/1P1BPN2/.text:
White develops, attempting to address the issue of us having so much influence over the central e4 square.

In reply we'll fianchetto.

rn1qkbnr/pbpp1ppp/1p2p3/8/3P4/1P3N2/PBP1.text:
White decides to play d4 and commit a pawn to the center.

We continue with the plan we've previously demonstrated, and take control of the e4 square.

rn1qkbnr/pbpp1ppp/1p2p3/8/3P4/4PN2/PPP1B.text:
White prepares to castle.

We will go for our idea of e4 control.

rn1qkbnr/pbpp1ppp/1p2p3/8/3PP3/2N2N2/PPP.text:
White goes for the Two Knights setup.

We develop, attacking one of them.

rn1qkbnr/pbpp2pp/1p2p3/5p2/3P4/1P3N2/PBP.text:
White can continue with normal development.

We'll continue to develop, controlling e4.

rn1qkbnr/pbpp2pp/1p2p3/5p2/3P4/4PN2/PPP1.text:
White castles.

And we will develop with an eye on e4.

rn1qkbnr/pbpppppp/1p6/8/3P4/4PN2/PPP2PPP.text:
White develops, controlling e5.

We'll open up lines for our other bishop by playing ...e6.

rn1qkbnr/pbpppppp/1p6/8/3PP3/2N5/PPP2PPP.text:
White supports their two central pawns with pieces.

We'll get ready to undermine one of the supporters of the pawn center.

rn1qkbnr/pbpppppp/1p6/8/8/1P3N2/PBPPPPPP.text:
White develops a knight to control central squares before committing any pawns.

We'll play as before.

rnbq1rk1/pp3ppp/2pb1n2/3pp3/4P3/3P1NP1/P.text:
White strikes in the center!

But we can ignore the push and just develop our rook, defending e5.

rnbq1rk1/ppp2ppp/3b1n2/3pp3/8/3P1NP1/PPP.text:
White prepares the thematic e4 push.

We'll lend support to our center with c6.

rnbqk2r/ppp2ppp/3b1n2/3pp3/8/3P1NP1/PPP1.text:
White castles.

We will do likewise.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/5n2/3pp3/8/3P1NP1/PPP1P.text:
White develops, placing pressure on our center.

We'll develop, supporting it.

rnbqkbnr/p1pppppp/1p6/8/3P4/4P3/PPP2PPP/.text:
White gains space in the center.

We will fianchetto.

rnbqkbnr/p1pppppp/1p6/8/4P3/2N5/PPPP1PPP.text:
White usually will play a second move which merely transposes into our previous chapters.

We fianchetto, as before.

rnbqkbnr/p1pppppp/1p6/8/8/1P6/PBPPPPPP/R.text:
White fianchettoes.

And so do we.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/3pp3/2P5/6P1/PP1PPPBP.text:
Or White can play c4 right away, with the idea of undermining our center and giving their bishop greater scope.

Here we can advance, gaining space.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/3pp3/8/3P2P1/PPP1PPBP.text:
White can go d3 in preparation of an e4 push.

We'll develop to f6, fighting for control of the central squares.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/4p3/2Pp4/3P2P1/PP2PPB.text:
White defends c4 and prevents our pawn from going further.

We'll proceed with normal development.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/8/6P1/PPPPPPBP/R.text:
White fianchettoes.

Here we can continue by gaining space and central control.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/1P6/P1PPPPPP/RNB.text:
Let's look at another offbeat move. 

White can start by fianchettoing their dark-squared bishop.

This doesn't interrupt our plan, so we'll go back to our queenside fianchetto.
